title: Trust, but Verify
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart borrows Derek Sivers's delegation parable from Anything You Want and turns it into a teaching maxim. Sivers hired an employee, drilled the one rule that mattered - every album, to every company, every week - and then stopped looking; months later the work was weeks behind and the employee was gone. The lesson Sivers drew, trust but verify, is the hinge of the piece. Stuart argues that teachers occupy the same structural position: we teach the work, repeat why it matters, build the conditions for motivation, and then trust students to do it - but trust without a verification loop is just hope. He converts this into three concrete checks: verify strategy use with low-stakes quizzing and polling, verify reading and writing with turn-in rates and spot checks of quality, and verify the curriculum itself by counting texts, prompts, and pop-up debates across the year. The closing move is about temperament rather than technique - when verification comes back negative, the response is to work the problem and improve the system, not to complain or throw up your hands.
points: Stuart's core move is to treat trust and verification as complementary rather than opposed - the verification exists precisely because the trust is genuine.

The three verification targets he names are usefully concrete: student use of learning strategies, turn-in rates and quality spot checks on the article of the week, and a running count of texts, writing prompts, and pop-up debates over the year.
Notably, the third check audits the teacher rather than the students - counting how much reading, writing, and speaking you actually assigned is a verification of your own curriculum claims.
Sivers's failure mode is instructive for teachers: repeating the priority in all caps and repeating it often still did not guarantee it was happening, because nothing was watching the output.
The piece ends on response discipline - a negative result is a systems problem to be worked, not an occasion for staffroom complaint.
quotes: Derek was running a company that helped musicians distribute their work, and one of the company's most important services was distributing albums to 50+ digital music retailers like iTunes and Amazon and Napster. But Derek realized that as long as he was the only one doing this, the company couldn't do its best work because his time wouldn't be spent on the creating and tinkering and innovating that he was best at.

So, he hired someone, trained the person, and, in all caps on the new employee's job agreement wrote “EVERY ALBUM, TO EVERY COMPANY, EVERY WEEK, NO MATTER WHAT.” He didn't cover the importance of this once — it was repeated, again and again and again.

We teach students to do the work it takes to master our disciplines. We repeat, again and again, in all kinds of ways, why and how this work matters. We do everything in our power to build classrooms where the five beliefs beneath motivation can grow.
And then we trust that kids do the work. But the verification bit is key, too.
So. Trust that students are using the learning strategies you've taught them — but verify with low-stakes quizzing and polling and informal conversation.
And when the verification comes back negative, don't throw up your hands. Don't run to a colleague to complain. Work the problem.
